# Summary: Richard Stallman
Richard Stallman (born March 16, 1953, New York City) is a pivotal figure in the free software movement and founder of the GNU Project. He showed early interest and talent in computing, programming at MIT's AI lab, where he developed influential software projects such as GNU Emacs and GCC, and published seminal work on intelligent backtracking in AI. Disturbed by the rise of proprietary software and restricted access to source code in the late 1970s and early 1980s, Stallman launched the GNU operating system in 1983, aiming to create a completely free and open-source alternative to Unix. He also founded the Free Software Foundation (FSF) to support these efforts and popularized the concept of copyleft, implementing it in the GNU General Public License (GPL).
Beyond his technical contributions, Stallman is a staunch activist for software freedom, digital rights, and ethical computing. He has campaigned extensively against software patents, DRM, and proprietary software, advocating for user freedoms grounded in moral values rather than just pragmatism. Stallman insists on precise terminology, promoting terms like "free software" and "GNU/Linux" to emphasize freedom and GNU's role. His uncompromising stance has often led to controversy, including public backlash over comments related to the Jeffrey Epstein scandal which precipitated his resignation from MIT and the FSF in 2019; he later returned to the FSF board in 2021. Stallman continues to be a vocal advocate for privacy, political activism related to open software, and ethical concerns around digital technology. He resides in Boston, has received numerous honors including the MacArthur Fellowship and memberships in prestigious academies, and remains influential in hacker culture and free software communities.
